body.heading: The motor in reverse
paragraphs: A generator is an electric motor run backwards. Instead of feeding in electricity to get turning, you feed in turning and get electricity out. Spin a coil of wire inside a magnetic field, and a voltage appears in the wire — the effect Michael Faraday demonstrated in 1831.

The voltage is induced because the magnetic field through the coil keeps changing as it rotates. Connect a circuit, and current flows. Push the coil around faster, or use stronger magnets and more turns of wire, and you generate more.

body.heading: From bicycle lamps to power stations
paragraphs: A bicycle dynamo is a pocket generator: the wheel spins a small magnet inside coils, making just enough electricity for the lamps. At the other extreme, power-station generators are metres across and produce electricity for whole cities.

What spins them varies — steam heated by coal, gas or nuclear reactions, falling water in a dam, wind turning a turbine, or a diesel engine in an emergency backup unit. The generator itself does not care; it simply converts whatever turning it receives. The conversion is silent, has no exhaust of its own, and works identically at every scale.

body.heading: Why the grid hums
paragraphs: Because the coil's voltage rises, falls and reverses as it spins, generators naturally produce alternating current — AC. Grid generators are carefully kept spinning in step, so the current everywhere alternates at a steady 50 or 60 times a second depending on the country.

That shared rhythm is a balancing act: at every moment, the electricity being generated must match what people are using. Grid operators watch demand constantly, spinning generators up or down to keep the frequency — and your lights — steady.
